I hope this helps, and I'll gladly provide any additional information or test anything if needed. --- ## Environment - OpenCode: Latest version - Platform: Windows Desktop - RAM: 16 GB - Model: DeepSeek (running inside OpenCode) ## Summary I have encountered the same issue three separate times. OpenCode suddenly creates approximately 100+ Node.js Runtime processes, memory usage reaches 99%, and Windows becomes completely unresponsive. Two of the three occurrences required a forced shutdown because the system completely froze. ## What I observed - The issue has occurred 3 times. - Memory usage reached 99%. - Around 100+ Node.js Runtime processes appeared under OpenCode. - Windows became completely unresponsive. - Mouse and keyboard stopped responding. - Task Manager was barely usable. - I had to force shutdown the PC twice. I have attached a screenshot showing: - 99% memory usage. - Approximately 108 OpenCode child processes. ## Additional observations One occurrence happened while DeepSeek was in the "Thinking" phase. I switched to another application, and when I came back, the issue had already started. After restarting Windows and opening OpenCode again (without sending any prompt), I noticed that the integrated terminal automatically runs: ```sh node scripts-dev/spike-host-probe.mjs ``` I don't know whether this is related to the issue, but I wanted to mention it. ## Notes I am using the Desktop version, so I could not follow the terminal-based heap snapshot instructions. If there is a way to generate a heap snapshot from the Desktop application, I would be happy to provide one. Thank you for your work. If you need any additional logs or if you'd like me to test a debug build, I'd be happy to help.

**"词元" literally means something like "linguistic unit."** And that’s exactly why some people think it’s not a proper translation of *token* in modern AI. Even in plain text LLMs, a token is not a real "word". It could be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or just a chunk of characters. The split depends on the tokenizer, not on natural linguistic boundaries.

With multimodal models, the mismatch is even clearer that we now have visual, image, audio, and video tokens, which may have nothing to do with language.

So I think "token" is better understood as **a basic unit a model processes**. "词元" only works in NLP, but as a general AI term, the "词" part can be misleading.

I experienced a similar infinite-loop/token-consumption issue with Claude Sonnet 4.6, although the behavior in my case appears to be slightly different from the empty-LLM-response loop described here.

### Environment

- OpenCode: 1.18.4
- Model: Claude Sonnet 4.6
- RTK: 0.44.2
- Helm: 3.21.3

### What happened

I asked OpenCode to analyze some changes in a local Helm repository.

During the analysis, OpenCode started repeatedly executing the same shell command:

    rtk helm plugin list

The command itself was NOT hanging. It completed successfully and returned:

    NAME    VERSION    DESCRIPTION

The OpenCode session nevertheless continued invoking the same operation repeatedly, resulting in an apparent tool-call loop.

This eventually consumed my entire daily token allowance before I could stop it.

### I investigated whether RTK/Helm was causing the loop

The RTK OpenCode plugin is installed at:

    ~/.config/opencode/plugins/rtk.ts

I verified that RTK rewrites the command as expected:

    $ rtk rewrite "helm plugin list"
    rtk helm plugin list

I also tested both commands independently:

    $ time helm plugin list
    NAME    VERSION    DESCRIPTION

    real    0m0.064s

and:

    $ time rtk helm plugin list
    NAME    VERSION    DESCRIPTION

    real    0m0.104s

Both commands complete normally.

The RTK plugin itself only calls `rtk rewrite` and replaces the command when the rewritten command differs from the original. I could not find anything in the plugin that would cause the command to execute repeatedly.

Therefore, at this point I suspect the loop is happening in the OpenCode/model tool-call cycle rather than in Helm or RTK.

### Why I'm reporting this here

The behavior seems related to the tool/session loop described in this issue, especially because Claude Sonnet 4.6 is also involved in my case.

However, my case differs in an important way: instead of repeated empty LLM calls after tool execution, I observed the agent repeatedly requesting the same successful tool operation.

This also raises a broader concern about loop protection: a single model/tool interaction should not be able to repeatedly execute an identical tool call indefinitely and consume an entire token quota.

Would this be considered the same underlying session-loop issue, or should this behavior be tracked separately?

A configurable safeguard such as detecting repeated identical tool calls (e.g. N consecutive identical calls without progress) could also help prevent this class of issue and protect users from uncontrolled token consumption.

The current behavior is worth calling out explicitly because it's not just "no worktree support" — it's actively misleading. The sidebar git label is resolved once at launch against the workspace root (the launch directory), via `git symbolic-ref --short HEAD`. That command is itself worktree-aware, but it's only ever run in the launch dir. So when I start opencode in the main repo and then create/enter a worktree to do branch work, the sidebar stays pinned at `projectname:main` for the entire session even though `git symbolic-ref` in the worktree correctly returns `feature/foo`.

The workflow we want this for: **create the worktree from inside opencode, and have the sidebar reflect the tree the session is actually operating in.** Today we launch opencode from the main repo and choose the launch directory up front, committing to it for the whole session. If `opencode worktree create` + the warp dialog move us between trees mid-session, the sidebar needs to follow, otherwise the label and the working tree disagree and the agent's mental model of "what branch am I on" comes from grepping `git branch` in bash output rather than the UI.

+1 to the scope as proposed — the stash-on-warp semantics are the right call for preserving uncommitted state. The one piece I'd add to the acceptance criteria: the sidebar label (and any status-bar branch indicator) must re-resolve from the *active* worktree, not the launch dir, after every warp.

Adding concrete numbers from a local context-bloat investigation — this is the top cause of context-window compaction on this host.

Evidence (mined from the local session DB):
- Single edit tool part reached **16.4 MB** (editing a ~7.8 MB runtime-bundle file) because the result carries full `state.metadata.filediff.before` + `.after` (~2x file size).
- Lifetime edit-tool result content across all sessions: **284.6 MB** — the largest per-tool contributor (~34% of ~843 MB stored tool content). Token cost is higher than byte cost since the same content is retokenized every turn.
- Worst session hit **18 compactions** (76 parts/compaction — context filling almost every turn); a ~120 KB config doc edited 30+ times in one session re-injected ~230 KB of before+after each time.

Why it's disproportionately bad: unlike other large outputs (bash/read), an edit's before+after is largely identical to content already in context (the caller just supplied old+new strings), so it's near-pure redundancy that accelerates compaction without adding information.

Suggested fix (confirming the original ask): stop persisting full filediff.before/.after into the model-facing message; keep only the diff field (already present) or cap snapshots to changed lines ±N. Store full before/after server-side for undo/revert only.

Workaround meanwhile implemented on our side: a pre-edit size guard (edit_guard.py) that blocks editing files > 100 KB and warns > 50 KB, plus a context_bloat_audit.py that flags edit-echo + compaction storms on demand.

Thanks for the report. This is expected behavior rather than an agent-config filtering bug.

`fallbacks` and `persona` are not supported agent configuration fields. Unrecognized fields in an agent definition are intentionally treated as provider-specific model options and passed through to the selected provider, as documented under [Agents → Additional](https://opencode.ai/docs/agents#additional). Console Go is therefore correctly rejecting these two options because its request schema does not recognize them.

For persona or system instructions, use the agent's supported `prompt` field. Native fallback across different models is not currently supported; that feature request is tracked separately in #7602, and adding a `fallbacks` field does not enable it.

Closing as not planned because OpenCode should continue forwarding provider-specific agent options.

Thanks for the report. `delegateTo` is not an internal OpenCode field, and OpenCode does not synthesize or use a field with that name for agent delegation.

Unrecognized fields in an agent definition are intentionally treated as provider-specific model options and passed through to the selected provider, as documented under [Agents → Additional](https://opencode.ai/docs/agents#additional). If `delegateTo` is present in an agent definition, plugin, or request transform, a strict provider will therefore reject it; it should be removed from that configuration.

The linked `instructions` and `promptCacheKey` issues were different: those concerned options OpenCode itself generated for particular provider paths. There is no equivalent OpenCode-generated `delegateTo` option to filter here.

Closing as not planned because OpenCode should continue forwarding provider-specific agent options.

There's a fix up for this now: #41463.

I hit the same root cause from a different angle — Vertex Gemini image models (`gemini-2.5-flash-image`) reject every request with `Unable to submit request because the model does not support function calling` — and filed #41464 before the duplicate bot pointed me here. Same cause you diagnosed: `capabilities.toolcall` is assigned in `provider.ts` and never read in the request path.

The patch is a guard in `resolveTools` (`session/llm/request.ts`), which is where every send path converges:

```ts
if (!input.model.capabilities.toolcall) return {}
```

Verified by capturing the outgoing provider request from a source build with the stock `build` agent and no config overrides: a `toolcall: false` model now sends no `tools` field at all (was 12 declarations), while a tool-calling model in the same session still sends all 12. Two tests added; I checked the negative one fails without the guard.

Worth noting this is the third report of the same thing — #19966 (closed by the 60-day inactivity bot rather than on merit), this issue, and #41464. @sbadakhc's morphllm/NVIDIA NIM cases should be covered by the same guard, since it drops the tools array before any provider-specific serialization.

Happy to fold #41464 into this issue if maintainers prefer one thread.

The duplicate bot on #41464 pointed me at prior reports of this exact root cause, which I'd missed:

- **#35432** (open, assigned) — "Config `tool_call: false` does not disable tools", filed 2026-07-05 against morphllm, with a second confirmation from @sbadakhc against NVIDIA NIM. Same diagnosis: `capabilities.toolcall` assigned in `provider.ts`, never read in the request path.
- **#19966** (closed 2026-07-03) — asked for precisely this change, closed by the 60-day inactivity bot rather than on merit.

So this is the fourth report and, as far as I can tell, the first patch. Three providers affected: Vertex Gemini image models, morphllm/vLLM without `--enable-auto-tool-choice`, and NVIDIA NIM. The guard sits in `resolveTools` before any provider-specific serialization, so all three are covered by the same line.

Happy to retarget this PR to close #35432 instead of #41464 (or both) — whichever keeps your tracker tidy. I've left a note on #35432 as well.
